abstract: Lysosomes are essential for cell survival but are highly susceptible to pathological stressors. Thus, the ability to initiate an acute damage response and promote recovery is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis. Although studies have advanced understanding of acute responses to lysosomal injury, the mechanisms governing the recovery stage and how this phase differs from the initial injury response remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a distinct response during the recovery stage. We provide the first evidence that recovery from acute damage triggers processing body (PB) formation, membraneless biomolecular condensates. Mechanistically, PBs are selectively induced during recovery, but not during acute damage, through interactions with stress granules (SGs), distinct membraneless biomolecular condensates formed upon acute injury. Functional analyses reveal that PBs promote lysosomal quality and cell survival by collaborating with SGs. Together, these findings establish PBs as central effectors of the lysosomal recovery program and underscore the broader relevance of biomolecular condensates in cellular responses to lysosomal damage and related diseases.
